title: Low-loss cryogenic interconnects for quantum processors
bottleneck: Wiring hundreds of qubits demands dense, low-thermal-conductivity, low-loss microwave cabling from room temperature to millikelvin stages, and existing coaxial looms are bulky, expensive, and a major heat load. Superconducting flex cables and photonic links are in development, but no solution yet combines the channel density, crosstalk isolation, and thermal performance needed for thousand-qubit machines. Interconnects are now a scaling bottleneck on par with the qubits themselves.
why_it_blocks: Quantum processors cannot grow past a few hundred qubits without a wiring solution that fits in a dilution refrigerator. The cabling wall forces awkward modular architectures and slows the road to error-corrected machines.
current_state: Superconducting flexible striplines and cryo-CMOS multiplexing are advancing in labs, and the 2026 materials-search pipeline may yield lower-loss conductor options. But a standardized, manufacturable high-density cryogenic interconnect does not yet exist.
